global.headline: ZELENSKY ENDS THE REFINERY PAUSE AS UKRAINE RUNS OUT OF PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS
summary: Zelensky told the Financial Times the pause on striking Russian energy, observed to meet an American demand, is over; Russia then accused Ukraine of hitting a refinery. He would hold off only for more interceptors “at a minimum”, and said that when he asked for air defences “the American response was to weaken Starlink’s service”.

A source told CNN Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors: “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.” That strike, overnight into Wednesday, hit three Kyiv power plants and Kharkiv energy sites, killing four and injuring 25; the air force’s four intercepts were apparently its last. In August Zelensky put holdings at a tenth of what was needed, and a promised US licence to build the missiles never materialised.

Starshield speeds were partly but not fully restored. Zelensky said Russia launched over 850 drones after midnight “at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted”. Republicans joined Democrats in asking the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate whether the administration caused the throttling. Britain’s Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Kyiv before meeting Pete Hegseth in Washington.
global.geopolitical: Kyiv has defied an American demand while dependent on American interceptors and an American-run satellite network — a bet that Washington’s leverage is already spent. The bipartisan referral matters more: it moves the Starshield question into oversight the White House does not control.
global.socioeconomic: An empty Patriot magazine means ballistic missiles reach Ukraine’s power plants essentially unopposed as the heating season starts, and PURL, the route Washington threatened to cut this week, is how replacements would arrive.

global.headline: HOUTHI MISSILES HIT YEMEN'S PRESIDENTIAL PALACE, AND WASHINGTON DRAWS UP A 'MOTHER OF ALL BOMBS' STRIKE ON IRAN
summary: Missiles and drones struck Aden’s al-Maashiq Palace, seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, killing five — two of them Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani’s bodyguards — and injuring 16. The prime minister and ministers were unhurt. The Houthis claimed a Saudi “war operations headquarters” inside the compound, treating any Saudi military presence as a legitimate target. They said Saudi Arabia flew 65 strikes across Yemen in 24 hours; Sanaa’s health ministry put the toll since 3 September at 120 killed and 307 wounded, about 60% women and children — unverifiable. Yemen’s military said it killed the Houthis’ missile and drone chief, Abu al-Fadl al-Hadrami.

CNN reported the Pentagon has built strike packages using the GBU-43/B MOAB against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites including Pickaxe Mountain, for use before or after 3 November; one source said such a strike would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR” — bomb, declare victory, withdraw. Officials doubt it reaches granite-shielded targets: “a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else”. Brent fell about 1.5% to US$104.40 (S$133.63) and WTI 1.2% to US$93.90 (S$120.19) as Washington weighed easing tanker shipping restrictions.
global.geopolitical: The Houthis reached the Yemeni government’s own seat while under the heaviest Saudi bombardment of the war, disposing of Riyadh’s remaining theory of victory — that enough pressure produces a truce. A bomb chosen for effect rather than penetration shows Washington shopping for an exit, not a military objective.
global.socioeconomic: Crude eased only on the prospect of American softening on tanker sanctions, not on anything that improved at sea; the premium still rests on a strait where two hulls went down this week.

global.headline: DRONES SET TWO TANKERS ALIGHT INSIDE ROMANIAN WATERS AND NATO REOPENS ITS BLACK SEA POSTURE
summary: The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader, sailing Tunisia to Romania, and the Yara J were hit by drones inside Romanian territorial waters late Wednesday and set ablaze. Seven of the Wine Trader’s crew are missing; all of the Yara J’s are safe. A NATO military source told Reuters the drones “were of Russian origin”. President Nicușor Dan would not assign blame: “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”

Dan met Bulgaria’s Rumen Radev and NATO’s Mark Rutte and agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”; Rutte said the alliance would adjust its “deterrence and defence posture as needed”, with the North Atlantic Council to take it up next week. Reuters counts at least 23 sailors killed or missing off the two countries in ten days, including 11 from the HS Dignity, hit Tuesday. Radev was blunter: “The results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians.” A draft EU summit text calls the attacks “a serious violation of international and maritime law”.
global.geopolitical: Strikes inside a NATO member’s territorial sea, attributed by NATO’s own source to Russia, are the closest this war has come to engaging collective defence, and the answer is a posture review. That is the message Moscow reads about where the line sits.
global.socioeconomic: The corridor under attack carries Ukrainian grain to market. War-risk cover for the Romanian and Bulgarian approaches reprices within days, and food importers far from the Black Sea pay it.

global.headline: A SCHOOL ROOF FALLS IN PESHAWAR AND KILLS 34 CHILDREN
summary: The roof of the privately run al-Khair school collapsed at 8.48am local time, crumpling two storeys into three classrooms holding 110 pupils. At least 34 children and a female teacher died — 12 of the dead were girls — and 45 children were injured, three critically. Most were under 13 and from low-income households; rescuers, some digging by hand, worked four to five hours.

Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed: “It was a weak building structure. Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse.” The owner has been arrested. Relatives said warnings were ignored. Pakistan spends under 1% of its roughly US$450 billion (S$576 billion) GDP on education, pushing families into low-cost private schools in rented, barely inspected buildings; 14 children died in a Lahore tutoring-centre collapse in June. The school stands in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where President Asif Ali Zardari imposed emergency rule on Sunday and installed a governor over Imran Khan’s party.
global.geopolitical: The collapse lands in the one province Islamabad has just taken direct control of, so findings about who failed to inspect the building feed the constitutional fight over whether the federal government or Khan's party is responsible for governing it.
global.socioeconomic: The gap between what the state spends on schooling and what families need is filled by unregulated private schools, and this is the price of it. Arresting one owner inspects none of the thousands of buildings like his.

global.headline: AMERICAN WHOLESALE INFLATION HITS A FOUR-YEAR HIGH AND THE CHIP TRADE BREAKS
summary: September’s Producer Price Index rose 1.3% on the month and 6.3% on the year against forecasts of 0.5% and 5.3% — the fastest month since March 2022 and highest annual rate since December 2022, a day after CPI hit 3.7%. Energy drove 80% of a record 2.9% jump in goods prices; core PPI rose 0.7% to 5% annually. Retail sales slowed to 0.8%, and 0.2% excluding petrol. RSM’s Joe Brusuelas noted the shock reaching food: vegetables up 41% on August, grains 17.4%, oilseeds 11.4%.

Asian chips broke first. The Kospi closed 7.6% lower, tripping a circuit breaker, SK Hynix down 11% and Samsung 9.5%; the Nikkei fell 4.9%. TSMC’s C.C. Wei warned of rising component prices despite strong earnings and the stock fell 2%. The semiconductor index fell a seventh straight day, down roughly 20% from June. Wall Street steadied as money left chips: the Dow rose 556 points, Treasury yields fell sharply. CoreWeave, carrying tens of billions in debt, fell 15.5% Wednesday then rose 6%; Gartner expects over 80% of “neocloud” providers to shut by 2030. Anthropic told investors sales grew 45% to US$17 billion (S$21.8 billion) last quarter after more than doubling in the second.
global.geopolitical: A fuel shock routed through a shipping chokepoint is now setting the American interest rate, which prices every borrowed dollar of the AI buildout. The line from Hormuz to the cost of a data centre has never been shorter.
global.socioeconomic: Producer prices lead consumer prices by months and the food components have turned, so the grocery bill tightens after the 3 November vote; leveraged AI borrowers meet the rate now.

global.headline: BRAZIL BANS THE SIX-DAY WEEK TEN DAYS BEFORE ITS RUNOFF
summary: Brazil’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment 75 to 1 — only Hamilton Mourão against — banning six-day working weeks and cutting the legal maximum from 44 hours to 40, after it passed the lower house in May. Sixteen million people work six days now; more than 30 million will see their maximum week fall, mostly low-paid retail, restaurant and hotel staff. It began as a TikTok campaign started by a pharmacy assistant.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who argued in May it would cause “mass unemployment”, reversed on Tuesday after polls showed over 70% support and more than half of his own voters in favour; Folha reported he told business leaders he would review parts of it if elected. Lula, trailing after the first round, said ending the “6x1” schedule means “more time to live, rest, be with family”. Nothing changes before the 25 October runoff: promulgation starts a 60-day clock to abolish six-day weeks and cut to 42 hours, with 40 following 14 months later.
global.geopolitical: A right-wing candidate holding a first-round lead and an incoming congressional majority still could not afford to vote against this, which marks the limit of what the Brazilian right can attempt on labour even from a winning position.
global.socioeconomic: Thirty million workers gain hours back; the cost falls on sectors running long rosters on thin margins, and the phasing means employers meet the bill long after the election it was timed for.

singapore.headline: PM WONG SAYS SINGAPORE IS IDENTIFYING THE COMPANIES BEHIND THE FIRES AS THE CENTRAL PSI HITS 224
summary: The 24-hour PSI in central Singapore reached 224 at 7am Friday, a new high for the year, having entered the very unhealthy band at midnight; the other four regions were unhealthy at 146 to 195, with hourly PM2.5 elevated across all five at 93 to 149. Thursday peaked at 212 in the west, where Wednesday’s hourly PM2.5 hit 288, a level not recorded since 2015.

PM Lawrence Wong said Singapore is looking into which companies may be responsible for the Indonesian forest and peatland fires: “Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and explore joint action with other countries.” That goes beyond Grace Fu’s 14 October line that options were open. A Greenpeace report on 5 October linked SGX-listed Bumitama Agri and First Resources, and privately held First Borneo Plantations, to areas where fires were detected. The 2014 Act allows fines of S$100,000 a day capped at S$2 million and has never been used.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said Jakarta will accept foreign help, with President Prabowo Subianto’s approval and details being settled at technical level — a reversal. Here, N95 distribution was brought forward and queues formed at community clubs, and ActiveSG shut outdoor facilities in the central, southern and western regions.
singapore.geopolitical: Naming companies shifts Singapore from requesting Indonesian cooperation to preparing to prosecute firms listed on its own exchange — the one lever needing nobody’s consent. Jakarta accepting help the same day is what makes the shift read as pressure rather than posture.
singapore.socioeconomic: Two of the three firms Greenpeace named are listed here, so liability would land on Singapore shareholders. Meanwhile a fourth day of very unhealthy air is paid in lost outdoor earnings, with delivery riders choosing between income and their lungs.

singapore.headline: VIVIAN BALAKRISHNAN WARNS AGAINST TECH RULES WRITTEN BY A FEW STATES AND FIRMS
summary: At Singapore International Cyber Week, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said the rules governing technologies that affect everyone “cannot be monopolised by a handful of powerful states and big tech companies”, and must include small and developing states because “even the superpowers will not have a monopoly on the complete technology stack”. He likened trillion-dollar technology firms to the British and Dutch East India Companies — private bodies outweighing most states — and warned AI in Ukraine and the Middle East is pushing “decisions to fire or not to fire” to machine speed.

OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said the firm backs Singapore’s call for AI incident transparency and will alert affected agencies immediately once confident an incident occurred — but set no deadline: “We are waiting to see if the Singapore Government is going to put an actual timeline on that.” Shanmugam made the request on 13 October, after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to an Australian Medicare statistics portal in June and Canberra was told only on 10 September, by email to a public mailbox. Lehane conceded the firm should have been faster.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is bidding to write the procedural layer of AI governance — incident reporting, model evaluation, testing standards — because that is the part a small state can supply when the substantive rules are set in a few boardrooms.
singapore.socioeconomic: Without a reporting clock a government learns its systems were breached when the vendor finishes investigating. That is the arrangement that left Australia uninformed for three months, and OpenAI has made the absence of a deadline its defence.

singapore.headline: TOURISM RECEIPTS FALL 6.2% AS THE WAR REACHES SINGAPORE'S VISITOR NUMBERS
summary: Second-quarter tourism receipts were S$7.21 billion, down 6.2% on the year and 15.4% on the first quarter’s S$8.51 billion, with arrivals down 6.6% to 3.76 million. The Tourism Board blamed the first-quarter escalation of the Middle East conflict for higher fuel costs, reduced air capacity and weaker demand “particularly from European source markets”. First-half receipts of S$15.71 billion were down only 0.3%, on 8.19 million arrivals.

Sightseeing, entertainment and gaming fell hardest, down 15.4% to S$1.58 billion, with the June-July World Cup pulling wagering towards sports betting; food and beverage fell 9.8%, accommodation 8.4%, shopping 1.5%. China led spending at S$965.5 million (down 1.9%), then Indonesia S$589.7 million (down 15.2%), Australia S$526.7 million (up 5.6%), India S$471.6 million (down 5.6%), the US S$427.2 million (up 16.1%).
singapore.geopolitical: A war 6,000km away arrives in Singapore's accounts as thinner European arrivals and dearer seats — the practical meaning of an economy that depends on other people's ability to fly.
singapore.socioeconomic: A 6.2% quarter is survivable; the composition is the warning. The steepest falls are in the most labour-intensive segments — attractions, restaurants, hotels — where hours are cut long before headcount.

word.definition: Wrongdoing, especially by a company or a public official acting in breach of a legal duty.
word.etymology: From Anglo-Norman French malfaisance, 'wrongdoing', from mal- ('badly', Latin male) and faisance ('doing', from faire, Latin facere); in English legal use from the 17th century.
word.example: Singapore moved from monitoring the haze to assigning blame for it, with PM Wong saying it is identifying which companies caused the Indonesian fires — the first step towards proving malfeasance under a law unused in twelve years.
